title: Previewing Hungary’s Election: Will Orbán Be Defeated?
transcriptText:
Hi, I'm Max Bergman. And I'm Donath
Enright. And this is The Euro File, a
podcast where we look at Europe through
a Washington lens.
We are thrilled to welcome Jacques
Chucky to The Euro File.
Jacques is senior research fellow at the
Center for European Reform, where her
work focuses on EU institutions,
elections, rule of law, and democracy.
She was previously policy leader fellow
at EUI, and very importantly, and that's
where I first read her work, research
director at Freedom House. Her expertise
on Hungary's democratic backsliding and
the challenges facing liberal democracy
in the region I think makes her the
perfect guest to preview what many,
including some of us here at CSIS, are
calling the most consequential election
in Europe this year. Jacques, welcome to
the show. Thank you. Glad to be here.
So, there's a lot going on. And every
day brings new news out of Hungary, but
basically, big picture here, on April
12th, Hungarians are going to the polls,
and as we said, it's a really
consequential election. But can you tell
us why it's portrayed that way, and why
is it such an important election? Yeah,
of course. I agree with you that this is
an important election, and not just
because I have been following Hungary
for very many years, let's just put it
that way. But also, I think for two
reasons. On the one hand, one is that it
is such a symbolic election because
Orban has been a standard bearer for
illiberalism for 16 years at this point.
In some sense, you know, he was Trump
before Trump. And so, a defeat for him
would have high symbolic value
and perhaps would signal a change in
trends. I like to think of Hungary as a
trendsetter, partly because its
democracy has been more fragile, and so
we could see things earlier in Hungary
than in other countries. [clears throat]
But it's unclear if this will work in
the other direction, as well.
The other reason I think it's important
is from an EU perspective because the EU
needs unanimity on certain issues,
mostly on issues related to foreign
policy.
And Orban has blocked files. And, up
until now, he has folded most of the
time on these files, whether that was
sanctions against Russian companies or
individuals or support for Ukraine. But
it doesn't look like that is happening
right now when it comes to the 90
billion loan to Ukraine. And so
going forward, Hungary seems to be much
more of a an obstructionist force in the
EU. It seems to be something that the EU
otherwise cannot handle.
And so, in that sense, this is certainly
in Europe is the most important election
this year.
Jacques, maybe you could give us some
background about why it appears that
Victor Orban is on the precipice of
losing. Why is he in trouble? When the
elections happened four years ago, there
was also a lot of attention and some
expectation that he could potentially
lose. He came out and won that election,
did so, you know, in a somewhat sturdy
fashion. And so, why is this time
different? And maybe to use another
comparison, you know, in Turkey with
Erdogan, there was also a lot of sense
that, okay, here's the opposition,
they're rallying. So, is this sort of a
false democratic dawn? What makes Tisza
and Peter Magyar different, or at least,
you know, the situation appears to be
very different now than it was four
years ago. Why is Orban in this sort of
weakened state? Yes, yes. So, I think
the parallel with four years ago is
important and is a useful starting point
because essentially, one key difference
this time is that we have a new
opposition. So, four years ago, we had a
united opposition, which meant all the
opposition, not all, but most of the
opposition parties that previously had
challenged Orban coordinated and ran in
a united way.
But those parties had been present in
Hungarian politics for some time, and
they had been unsuccessful before.
This time, we have a a new actor, Peter
Magyar, as you mentioned, and his Tisza
Party. He appeared on the scene two
years ago. So, a very new actor whose
promises is quite different, or somewhat
different from the previous opposition
parties. I mean, he's he promises that
he's not Orban. In that sense, it's
similar to the rest of the previous
opposition. But otherwise, his ideology
and his background is different. He's a
more conservative politician, and he
comes from
Fidesz, or a former Fidesz affiliate.
So, that is
one difference. The other difference is
the economy. And I think we shouldn't
underestimate the importance of this.
Because essentially, Fidesz had been
riding on an economic
growth for 10 plus years.
And that is no longer the case. So,
after COVID and then after the war broke
out, Hungary's economy started
smell Let's just say it sputtering.
And if we compare with the previous
cycles, essentially, this is the first
time, this is the first four-year cycle
where there has been no GDP growth, or
close to zero.
Previously, you know there was growth as
much as 13%.
And so, this really matters because it
means that people don't necessarily feel
like that their lives are improving.
And Hungary's inflation was among the I
think it was the highest in the EU two
years ago. So, in fact, it's not just
that they don't feel that their lives
are improving, but what they are feeling
is that everyday life has become harder.
I would say that these are the two key
differences that allow the opposition,
or Peter Magyar, to really have a shot
at winning this time. Observing from the
outside, the corollary to this economic
stagnation also seems to be that there's
more access to at least information
about how other people are doing really
well in Hungary. People around Orban in
particular, or his friend from school,
his son-in-law, all the people who are
getting contracts while people see their
own paychecks not getting them as far.
I'd love to hear a little bit more your
description of how Orban has
consolidated not just political power,
but also economic power over the last 16
years because often times when we think
about corrupt systems, corruption is
upstream of a lot of degradation of
public services, things that we're
hearing about Hungary on the hospital
system, for example, health care. So,
can you walk us through how that has
happened? Right. So, I mean, corruption
has been an important part of the story,
but I would say that up until now
corruption has often been seen as a fact
of life in Hungary, and so up until now,
it was not something that politically
opposition parties or leaders could
really take advantage of.
Because
I think I would say that there has been
a kind of a a tacit agreement between
some voters and Fidesz that, you know
there is something that is left over in
people's pockets, and then there is
something that goes into Fidesz's
pockets. And as long as
there is something in people's pockets,
they are willing to overlook that.
And I think the issue is that,
right now, it seems like that that
agreement is no longer working.
And so, that's why corruption is playing
a more important part. But
I don't want to say with this that
corruption has that it's not important.
And certainly, what Orban has done is
that he has centralized corruption. So
corruption previously was part of
Hungary's political system but it was
more decentralized. And Orban changed
that and really started channeling money
into building up essentially this
hinterland.
And that consists partly of loyal
businessman and as you mentioned
acquaintances, friends, family members
of Orban.
In fact, I think a few days ago, the FT
published a good article that showed
that um
between, I think in the past 16 years
loyal businessman have received
contracts to the tune of
28 billion euros
which is a massive sum. I think in fact
this is almost equal to the money that
Hungary
has received in the last seven-year
period from the EU.
Now, obviously, this is not all from EU
money. This is also from Hungarian state
contracts. But it just really shows you
the amount of funding that has been
channeled into essentially building up
this hinterland.
And so
this kind of economic power outside
political power
is something that was unknown, or was
unknown in Hungary before.
I think it's more similar to countries
like Georgia in the South Caucasus.
And this is certainly a question that if
there is a change in power, what happens
to this economic power that had been
amassed.
And
I think it's unclear at this point what
could be done with the money.
Let's maybe turn to the election.
Hungary has gotten a ton of attention
here in the United States, really over
the last decade, that kind of
organization of America is sometimes
talked about with the Trump
administration with kind of an illiberal
government here in the US trying to roll
back democracy, at least that's the
accusation. But it seems like we have
Magyar really emerging despite the fact
that the political playing field is sort
of tilted against him. This is an
election that seems like it kind of has
everything in terms of, you know,
dramatic scandals like Hollywood can
make a field day. There's Russian
interference allegations of Russian
interference. There's talk of sex tapes.
There's, you know, the intelligence
services getting involved. What is
happening right now in the election?
Maybe give us a state of the race. How
is this playing out? Is Orban, you know,
making gains? Or is any of the punches
that he's trying to land against Magyar,
are they landing? It's It feels like
Magyar is sort of very much sort of
deflecting everything that's coming at
him. Maybe describe what's happening in
the race currently. I mean, I agree with
you that it it feels like there's
something happening every day and there
is a new scandal that is taking place. I
think it was at the same time expected
because we are really in the home
stretch, in the final, you know,
few days, weeks. And I also think that
in that sense it's not dissimilar to
other elections, other recent elections.
I mean, if you think of Romania's
presidential election that was in the
end cancelled,
which resulted in a massive shift at the
very last moment. I think, sadly, this
is the new reality that we are seeing
these days. That elections are filled
with scandals, with
AI videos, with smear campaigns, with
potentially sex tapes. So, in that
sense, I don't think the Hungarian
election is an exception.
As you mentioned, we are seeing foreign
interference.
In that sense, it's somewhat of an
exception, obviously, because it looks
like that foreign interference is
favoring the governing party.
And that certainly
hasn't been the case in the other
countries mentioned.
I think, I mean, today's big news is
that a new or the last poll from Median,
the most accurate pollster, came out.
And Median was the pollster that came
closest to the end result 4 years ago.
And so this time around, they predict a
massive Tisza win, more than 20
percentage points advantage for Tisza,
which is in line with their previous
poll that came out at the end of
January, I believe, but is not
necessarily in line with other
pollsters.
This was certainly surprising, I think,
to many.
I myself, I'm a little bit more
cautious. I think the race is a bit
closer,
but it looks like
when it comes to all these attacks, that
they are not necessarily working on
Magyar. He has certain kind of Teflon
qualities.
And that is certainly an exception. So,
it looks like the two electorates are
really set in their ways.
And uh
we may not expect a lot of last-minute
change.
But I think
we are still 2 weeks away, I think, from
the vote at this point. So, I would wait
until the very last moment to be able to
say who seems to be closer to winning.
Can I just ask quickly about the role of
Ukraine?
Orban sort of trying to run as sort of
the peace candidate, fights over the
pipeline that comes from Russia through
Ukraine into Hungary that has been
damaged. And And this is, you know, the
justification for blocking EU aid to
Ukraine.
How is that resonating inside of
Hungary? What is the role of Ukraine in
this election?
Ukraine is essentially the enemy that
Fidesz is using in this election because
Fidesz's campaign has been built around
{quote} enemies in previous years as
well, during previous elections as well.
And so we saw that the migrant crisis
around 2016 and after during the 2018
elections, we saw that with George
Soros, who was the main {quote} foreign
enemy in the 2022 election and
beforehand. And it looks like that role
is now given to Ukraine and President
Zelensky because he symbolizes the war
in a sense for Fidesz voters and the way
that Orban is presenting the whole
conflict. And so this is something that
seems to resonate with Fidesz voters.
At this point, it doesn't look like that
it resonates with Tisza voters.
Although I would say Peter Magyar is not
exactly very friendly towards Ukraine.
He seems to be
more pragmatic on Ukraine and his
program on the foreign policy part of
his program, in fact, said that Hungary
doesn't agree with the accelerated
accession for Ukraine and that Hungary
would call a referendum on Ukraine's
accession to the European Union.
So, in that sense, he has
taken a more pragmatic/skeptical
stance on Ukraine. And I think that is
partly because
at this point, if he wants to reach
Fidesz voters, obviously he cannot be
supportive of Ukraine. But this This is
one of the main campaign topics. The
other is obviously living standards. And
as long as Fidesz can keep the focus on
foreign policy,
it has a shot at winning or a much
better shot at winning
than if the focus was much more on
issues around living standards.
We've also seen a lot of reporting, Max
alluded to that too, about Russia's
actions or interference in the election
at the moment. We're seeing a lot of
support from the US administration.
Obviously, President Trump has sent two
different endorsements for Orban. We
know that the Vice President might
travel to Budapest
pretty soon, a little bit before the
election.
How important do you think the role of
these actors is in the campaign? Is it
resonating with voters? And I'm curious
in particular if you have any thoughts
about what Magyar's relationship with
Washington would be.
So, I think on the role of these visits,
I don't think this kind of foreign
policy-related topics that they resonate
with voters outside of Fidesz's core
electorate.
For them, obviously, it's important that
Orban is this global player. And, you
know, just a few days ago, many of the
far-right leaders visited Hungary, from
Marine Le Pen to Abascal and everyone
else. And so, for Fidesz's core
electorate, you know, this is a sign of
strength that people are coming to
Viktor Orban and he is still a global
player that matters.
Otherwise, I think, I mean, you
mentioned that there might be a visit by
J.D. Vance. If that happens, I don't
think that that will make a massive
difference
because, I mean, Trump has already
expressed his support for Orban several
times. And that is
not really the question that is on
voters' minds.
You know, they They tend to focus on
domestic issues or the war. So, there
are these two key topics.
When it comes to your question on
Magyar's relationship with the US,
actually, I mean, that's a very
interesting question because I don't
think we have seen much on that.
So, when it comes to Tisza's foreign
policy,
their current foreign policy lead is
Anita Orban, no relation to Viktor
Orban, who comes from the private
sector, but previously worked for Fidesz
at at a point. She's conservative and
she worked on energy diversification.
And so, I think she would
probably have the ability to have a good
relationship with the US government. But
then, of course, that also depends on
openness on the [clears throat] side of
the US government. Otherwise, Magyar did
not say much about the US. And Anita
Orban also focused mostly on Hungary's
neighbors, so the regional relationship
and EU funds in the foreign policy part
of Tisza's program. So, there wasn't a
lot of discussion on this relationship.
Maybe just a quick follow-up there. Is
Trump popular in Hungary? I mean, we've
sort of been seeing the {quote} Trump
effect in various elections around the
world. You know, Canada was was the most
evident where the liberals sort of were
destined for defeat, then Trump got sort
of involved in the election. Now, Mark
Carney is Prime Minister of Canada. And
so, I'm curious, you know, is Trump
popular at all in Hungary? Does that
help Orban? And then also, if you could
talk a bit about the Russian role. And
how's that playing? Is that a concern?
There's been reports about Russian
actors on the ground from the Kremlin to
try to use political interference
mechanisms to support Orban. How do you
see that playing out? I mean, so neither
Trump nor Putin are very popular in
Hungary. I think that's um obviously
among, again, Fidesz's core electorate,
Trump is somewhat popular.
Putin, not so much, but more popular, I
think, than Zelensky.
But these are not necessarily the most
important parts. I think at the same
time there is this curious effect that
Trump's presidency hasn't necessarily
been the boon to Hungary that Orban
announced, that he heralded, and that he
expected.
Because when it comes to the economy,
tariffs have hurt Hungary's economic
prospects, obviously. And then, I mean,
the current energy crisis is certainly
not something that is good for Hungary's
economy.
There is also a double taxation treaty
that the Biden administration withdrew
with Hungary, and there is no movement
on that either. So, that double taxation
treaty is is missing.
And then, I think
I mean, Orbán has received some US
pressure on energy diversification.
And I think there was an announcement of
signing um small and medium-sized
reactors.
So, it's not just this obvious Trump has
been such a big win for Orbán. Not at
all, especially if you look at the
details.
But then, of course,
what resonates with voters and at the
symbolic level, that's a completely
different question.
When it comes to Russia and Russia's
role,
so, as you mentioned, so we are seeing a
lot of active interference right now by
Russia.
There was reporting of three GRU agents
being sent to Hungary under diplomatic
cover.
There was this Washington Post article
that was published just a few days ago
about a planned assassination attempt
against Orbán.
We are seeing this information
circulating also about this quote
unquote assassination attempt despite
the publication of the Washington Post
article.
And then, there was this curious case of
seizure of Ukrainian money transfer.
And then, of course, there is the
bombing of the Druzhba pipeline, which I
would fit into the same line,
which was done by Russia.
And so, we are seeing a lot of
attempts at interference. Obviously,
I think these attempts
they matter if the result ends up being
close.
Because then, they can perhaps shift
at maximum a few percentage points,
perhaps.
But really, a lot depends on framing,
how many people are reached by these
attempts, [clears throat]
then, you know, whether political actors
can frame them right before the
election.
If the result is not close, then they
will not make that much of a difference.
And I would say if people want to read
more about the seizure of this Ukrainian
money, there's an amazing investigation
by V Square that is such a crazy story.
But now, we're going to ask you to pull
out your crystal ball
since we're just a few weeks away from
the election, and think about some
scenarios for what could be happening.
Can you walk us through what you think
is in the realm of possible and the
impact that that could have, even just
interference like on election day,
accepting the results, disputing the
results? What do you think is possible?
So, there are a lot of possibilities.
So, based on this Median poll, I think
it seems, at least right now, that what
is more probable is a Tisza victory.
But a lot will depend on the um scale of
that victory.
I think if it's a comfortable majority,
and of course, if it's a supermajority,
then there is a chance of actual change
afterwards, and I find in that scenario
unlikely that Fidesz would be unwilling
to give up power.
Because that just shows that uh Tisza
has such popular support that it just
doesn't make sense in that case for
Fidesz to try to hold on to power.
Now, I think an equally likely scenario,
and this um
flies in the face of the mentioned
Median poll, but perhaps because I'm too
cautious, is that we have either a
narrow Tisza majority
or that we have
a scenario in in which there is no clear
winner, or at least we have to wait at
least a week to count votes that arrive
from outside Hungary's borders, which
will be counted the week after the the
election, or at least that is the end of
the counting period.
And I think I would also add that um and
listeners should keep this in mind that
right now, there is a state of emergency
in Hungary, and that state of emergency
ends a month after the election, and
that it can take up to a month for the
new parliament to start working.
And so, there is this period right after
the election where
in theory, Fidesz, or the if it's an
outgoing government, could still do
things.
Now, obviously, for them to do things,
it it only makes sense if the result is
very close.
And I don't want to go into um
very crazy scenario building, but
theoretically, they could also change
the constitution and make Orbán
president. I think that's unlikely, but
theoretically, it's possible.
I think
what may be more likely in that scenario
is that we have a chaotic period,
chaotic few weeks,
and a lot of political wrangling,
further polarization,
and that
in that case, even if Tisza wins, if
it's a narrow majority, then Fidesz will
work on coming back as soon as possible.
And there are certain ways for Fidesz to
undermine a a new Tisza government.
These include, for example, the
president sending laws to the
Constitutional Court. The president is a
Fidesz ally. The Constitutional Court is
stacked with Fidesz allies.
This is not a veto power, so the
Constitutional Court, in that case, has
to make a decision in 30 days,
but these could, you know, slow down
lawmaking.
And then, there are certain ways to
trigger early elections, but that would
come later with the adoption of the
budget next year.
So, I think
this would be my other plausible
scenario, that there is a um
either no clear winner or a narrow Tisza
majority, in which case
we may not see for a few weeks what
happens,
and then we may have a very difficult
period with a government that is um
perhaps not as stable as uh as people
would like it to be.
Let me ask you, because, you know, one
of the things that I've been
hearing in sort of discussions with some
Hungary watchers, often times not
Hungarian, but look at this situation,
look at the palace that Viktor Orbán has
sort of built for himself outside of
Budapest, look at the corruption that we
sort of talked about and how you have
this entire, you know, for more than a
decade, a kind of corrupt system built
around him, and say this is a guy that
can't lose. And not that he can't lose
the election, but like he can't go. And
if he goes, then he is opening himself
up to potential prosecution, in the same
way that we've seen in Russia and other
places, that you created a corrupt
dynamic in which it's all or nothing.
And so, you pause it from that and then
say, "Okay, uh you know, all the stops
are going to be pulled out. This will
not be a free and fair election.
There'll be cheating, there'll be
whatever it may be, that this is going
to be a fraudulent election, but that he
will hold on to power any means
necessary."
So, the question for you is, what do you
think about that scenario? What is right
or wrong with that scenario? The other
thing I've heard is that, you know, this
is the Austro-Hungarian bureaucracy, and
like no, they will There's no sort of
ability to cheat. But if there is sort
cheating or manipulation or other
action, you know, there is this country
next door to Hungary that, you know, had
a similar situation in 2004 with the
Orange Revolution in Ukraine and the
Maidan Revolution.
What do you think about that sort of
outright theft of the election? And
then,
is that plausible and what do you think
the reaction would be?
So, I think fraud on election day is
unlikely. I think that this will be a
free, but unfair election. Unfair
because of all the advantages that
Fidesz has.
But at least based on previous
elections, fraud it isn't happening on
election day. It is what goes into the
sausage, essentially. It is what happens
in the run-up to the vote.
Because 4 years ago, there were civil
society monitors in every district, and
it turned out that there were
irregularities, there were problems, but
there was no, you know, large-scale
cheating. So, in that sense, Orbán
cannot pull out all the stops.
At the same time, I mean, I agree with
you that he has a lot to lose,
and he cannot necessarily just afford to
leave. At the same time, I think where
the logic of
this explanation that you posited goes
awry is that
or at least I believe that if Orbán is
defeated by a popular majority, by
enough people,
then I don't see him clinging on to
power.
I think in that scenario, he would
leave, and he would hope to come back.
And, you know, I mean, we have seen
comebacks from politicians in the
region. I mean, Robert Fico is back in
power. Andrej Babiš is back in power.
Obviously, they had not rigged the
system to the same extent, but and then
next year, perhaps, Law and Justice will
be back in power.
So, I think it's just more logical in
that scenario for Orbán to make life as
hard as possible for the new government,
and then come back, and then perhaps,
you know, be in power for another 10,
15, 16 years.
So, in that sense, you know, Hungary is
not Belarus, and I think that is still a
difference, and is a meaningful
difference.
I think that's a pretty hopeful message
to leave this conversation on. Jacob,
thank you so much. There's so much more
we could be talking about, but hopefully
we can stay in touch ahead of the
election and afterwards as the the group
of observers that we are and waiting
eagerly for the result. Thank you.

segments.text: Hi, I'm Max Bergman. And I'm Donath Enright. And this is The Euro File, a podcast where we look at Europe through a Washington lens. We are thrilled to welcome Jacques Chucky to The Euro File. Jacques is senior research fellow at the

Center for European Reform, where her work focuses on EU institutions, elections, rule of law, and democracy. She was previously policy leader fellow at EUI, and very importantly, and that's where I first read her work, research

director at Freedom House. Her expertise on Hungary's democratic backsliding and the challenges facing liberal democracy in the region I think makes her the perfect guest to preview what many, including some of us here at CSIS, are

calling the most consequential election in Europe this year. Jacques, welcome to the show. Thank you. Glad to be here. So, there's a lot going on. And every day brings new news out of Hungary, but basically, big picture here, on April

12th, Hungarians are going to the polls, and as we said, it's a really consequential election. But can you tell us why it's portrayed that way, and why is it such an important election? Yeah, of course. I agree with you that this is

an important election, and not just because I have been following Hungary for very many years, let's just put it that way. But also, I think for two reasons. On the one hand, one is that it is such a symbolic election because

Orban has been a standard bearer for illiberalism for 16 years at this point. In some sense, you know, he was Trump before Trump. And so, a defeat for him would have high symbolic value and perhaps would signal a change in

trends. I like to think of Hungary as a trendsetter, partly because its democracy has been more fragile, and so we could see things earlier in Hungary than in other countries. [clears throat] But it's unclear if this will work in the other direction, as well.
